<!-- section:why -->

A setting or a compositional rule is useful only when it serves your intention. This lesson helps you explain a choice and inspect its consequence.

<!-- section:understand -->

Exposure concerns light reaching the sensor over time. Display brightness also depends on signal gain and rendering. Raising ISO does not itself admit more light through the lens. Compare files on the same display with identical rendering settings when possible. Name what changed before interpreting a result.

<!-- section:see -->

In a fictional still-life experiment, keep the lamp, aperture, and shutter duration fixed while changing ISO. The rendered image may look brighter, but the lens admitted the same light. This explains why brightness alone cannot tell you how much light was captured.

<!-- section:deeper -->

Avoid an absolute claim that higher ISO always causes worse visible noise. Scene exposure, sensor behavior, processing, and output all affect the result.

<!-- section:customer -->

We can brighten the displayed result without gathering more light; first ask whether the photograph needs a different capture or a different rendering.

<!-- section:try -->

Two images look equally bright. One used less light at capture and more gain. Can brightness prove equal exposure?

<!-- section:revisit -->

No. Equal display brightness does not establish equal captured light. Record scene light, aperture, time, gain, and rendering before comparing quality.
